intro:
It is a Saturday night in February and Las Olas Boulevard is buzzing. Snowbirds who flew in to escape the cold, boaters who tied up along the Intracoastal, and tourists drifting in from the beach are all looking for somewhere to eat. Dozens of restaurants sit within a few blocks of each other, and most of the people walking past your door have never heard of you. They are deciding where to eat right now, on their phones, by searching and reading reviews. Then April turns to May, the snowbirds head home, the boat traffic thins out, and those same tables sit half empty on a Tuesday.

That swing is the real challenge of running a restaurant in Fort Lauderdale. You are not just competing with the spot next door. You are trying to get found by visitors who do not know the city, win them over in the few seconds they spend on their phone, and then keep your dining room full when the crowds leave town. It is a different job than marketing a neighborhood spot that lives on regulars.

This guide is for owners who are tired of guessing. We will cover what actually makes marketing a restaurant in Fort Lauderdale different, what your restaurant really needs from marketing here, what to look for in a restaurant marketing agency in Fort Lauderdale, and how our team at Button Up Media helps local restaurants turn searches, scrolls, and season into booked tables.

sections.h2: What makes marketing a Fort Lauderdale restaurant different?
sections.html:
People love to say Fort Lauderdale is just a quieter Miami. If you run a restaurant here, you know that is not true. The marketing problem is its own animal, and it comes down to a few things you will not find in the same mix anywhere else.

The water is your front door, and a lot of guests arrive by it. Fort Lauderdale calls itself the Yachting Capital of the World, and it earns the name. The Intracoastal, the New River, and the canals mean your guests are not only coming off the street. Some of them are tying up at a dock. Waterfront rooms from Las Olas to the beach compete on views as much as food, so your photos and your online presence have to sell the whole experience, not just the plate.

The competition sits shoulder to shoulder. Las Olas Boulevard alone packs roughly three dozen bistros and restaurants into a short, walkable strip from the beach to the Intracoastal. Himmarshee and the downtown Riverwalk add more. A hungry visitor can see five options from one corner. Being the best food on the block does not help if the person scrolling their phone never lands on your name.

Your crowd changes with the calendar. This is the big one. Peak season runs roughly December through April, when snowbirds (including a large wave of Canadians) settle in for weeks or months, and tourists fill the hotels. Then the shoulder months arrive and the pace drops. A restaurant that only markets when it is already busy leaves money on the table in season and struggles to fill seats out of it.

Your guests are a true mix. On one night you are serving an out-of-state family, a table of boaters, a Canadian couple down for the winter, and locals who have lived in Broward for decades and speak Spanish at home. That mix is why a one-language, one-note approach falls flat here.

The neighborhoods are not interchangeable. An upscale room on Las Olas, a lively spot in the historic Himmarshee nightlife district, a trendy cafe in Flagler Village and the FAT Village arts area, and a beachfront place off A1A are all marketing to different people in different moods. The message that works for one misses the others.

sections.h2: What does a Fort Lauderdale restaurant actually need from marketing?
sections.html:
Forget the buzzwords for a minute. In this city, a handful of things do almost all the heavy lifting. Here is what matters, in plain terms.

  • A Google Business Profile that wins 'near me.' When a tourist on the beach or a boater at the dock types 'waterfront restaurant near me' or 'best dinner Fort Lauderdale,' Google decides who shows up on the map. Your profile, your categories, your photos, and your reviews decide whether that is you or the place down the street. For a restaurant that lives on visitors, this is the single most valuable thing to get right.
  • Reviews, and replies to them. Visitors who do not know the city lean hard on reviews. A steady flow of fresh, strong reviews, with real replies (in English and Spanish), is often the deciding factor between two patios on the same block.
  • Social content that sells the experience. Food, yes, but also the water, the patio, the golden hour, the vibe. Short video does the heavy lifting now. Good content gives a visitor a reason to choose you and gives a local a reason to come back.
  • A website that works on a phone. Nearly every visitor checks you on their phone first. They want the menu, hours, a photo, a map, and a way to book or find parking (or dockage) in a few taps. A slow or clunky site quietly sends people elsewhere.
  • Ads that turn the season on and off. Google and Meta ads let you push hard when visitors flood in and lean on locals to fill the slower months. Done right, ads are how you stop leaving season money on the table and how you survive the quiet weeks.

You do not need all of this perfect on day one. You need a partner who knows which lever to pull first for your room, your neighborhood, and the time of year.

sections.h2: How should a Fort Lauderdale restaurant market around the season and the big events?
sections.html:
In most cities, marketing is a steady hum. In Fort Lauderdale, it has a rhythm, and smart owners plan to it instead of reacting a week too late.

Build the foundation before season, not during it. The months before the December to April rush are when you want your Google profile polished, your reviews flowing, your photos fresh, and your ads tested. When the snowbirds and tourists arrive, the machine is already running and you are capturing demand instead of scrambling.

Treat the big moments as real opportunities. The Fort Lauderdale International Boat Show in the fall brings a wave of out-of-town visitors and the largest in-water boat show in the world to the marinas. The Winterfest Boat Parade in December draws huge crowds along the water. Tortuga Music Festival on the beach in the spring pulls thousands more. Each one is a chance to run a themed promotion, a timed ad push, and content aimed at people who are in town and looking for somewhere to eat tonight.

Do not go dark in the shoulder season. May through November is when a lot of restaurants quietly disappear online, which is exactly when leaning on locals pays off. Loyalty offers, slow-night promotions, and content aimed at Broward residents (in both languages) keep your dining room from feeling the drop as hard. The goal is a flatter, steadier year, not a feast-and-famine cycle you just hope to survive.

This kind of planning is hard to do off the side of your desk during service. It is a big part of what a local agency actually earns its fee doing.

sections.h2: Do you really need a local agency, or will any agency do?
sections.html:
Plenty of agencies will happily take a Fort Lauderdale restaurant's money from an office three states away. Some of the work they do (posting, basic ads) is not location-specific, and that is fine. But the parts that move the needle most here are deeply local.

An out-of-town team does not feel the season in its bones. It does not know that a Las Olas room and a Flagler Village cafe are marketing to different crowds, that a huge share of your best nights come from people who arrived by boat or plane, or that half your neighborhood reads reviews in Spanish. It will not naturally build your year around the Boat Show, Winterfest, and the snowbird calendar, because it does not live here.

You do not need a local agency for everything. But for the Google Business Profile, the local SEO, the bilingual content, and the seasonal planning that actually fill a Fort Lauderdale dining room, local knowledge is the difference between marketing that looks busy and marketing that books tables. That is the gap we are built to close.

That means loyalty offers, slow-night and happy-hour promotions, content aimed at Broward residents in both languages, and ads targeted at people who live here year-round. The restaurants that plan for the quiet months ahead of time have a far flatter, steadier year than the ones that only market when they are already full.

faqs.q: How should a waterfront restaurant market to boaters and tourists?

Strong, recent reviews matter even more with people who do not know the city. Tying promotions to big waterfront moments like the Boat Show and Winterfest helps you catch visitors when they are actively looking for somewhere to eat.

faqs.q: How long does restaurant marketing take to work in Fort Lauderdale?
